expect:

value: Momentum before = 1400 × 15 = 21 000 kg m/s [1 mark]. Combined mass = 2 400 kg [1 mark]. Velocity = 21 000 ÷ 2 400 = 8.75 m/s [1 mark]. expect: A wind turbine generates 500 000 J of electrical energy from 750 000 J of wind energy in a given time period. Calculate the efficiency of the turbine. Evaluate whether this is a reasonable efficiency for a large-scale energy generation device, and describe two ways engineers could try to improve energy efficiency in the overall electricity supply system.
value: A wind turbine generates 500 000 J of electrical energy from 1 250 000 J of wind energy in a given time period. Calculate the efficiency of the turbine. Evaluate whether this is a reasonable efficiency for a large-scale energy generation device, and describe two ways engineers could try to improve energy efficiency in the overall electricity supply system.
note: F21: 67% is above the Betz limit (about 59%), so no wind turbine can reach it; 40% is realistic.

expect: Efficiency = 500 000 ÷ 750 000 = 0.67 = 67% [1 mark]. Mastering (5–6): Good efficiency for wind (typical range 35–50% — note: 67% is an exam-context figure, not a real-world claim); any energy conversion will have some loss due to friction in moving parts, air resistance and heat in generator coils. Improvement methods evaluated: reducing friction in bearings via lubrication; using higher-voltage transmission lines to reduce resistance heating losses; improving generator coil efficiency. Conclusion evaluates trade-offs (cost vs benefit of each improvement). Secure (3–4): Correct efficiency calculation plus 2 improvement methods with partial reasoning. Developing (1–2): Correct efficiency calculation only.
value: Efficiency = 500 000 ÷ 1 250 000 = 0.4 = 40% [1 mark]. Mastering (5–6): 40% is typical for a large wind turbine (real turbines reach roughly 35–50%); any energy conversion loses some energy through friction in moving parts, air resistance and heating in the generator coils. Improvement methods evaluated: reducing friction in bearings via lubrication; using higher-voltage transmission lines to reduce resistance heating losses; improving generator coil efficiency. Conclusion evaluates trade-offs (cost vs benefit of each improvement). Secure (3–4): Correct efficiency calculation plus 2 improvement methods with partial reasoning. Developing (1–2): Correct efficiency calculation only.
note: F21: recomputed for the new figures and the author's aside removed.
